note: Source says "unprecedentedly free from sickness"; "unusually" weakens it.
replacement: That year, by general admission, was otherwise unprecedentedly free from sickness, and the few ordinary cases that did occur all ended in this disease. As a rule, however, there was no visible cause. People in good health were suddenly seized by violent heats in the head, with redness and inflammation of the eyes. The inward parts, such as the throat and tongue, turned bloody and gave off an unnatural, foul breath. Sneezing and hoarseness followed, and soon the pain reached the chest and brought on a hard cough. When it settled in the stomach, it upset it, and there came discharges of bile of every kind that physicians have named, with very great distress. In most cases an ineffectual retching followed, causing violent spasms; in some these ended soon afterward, in others much later. Outwardly the body was not very hot to the touch, nor pale, but reddish and livid, breaking out in small pustules and ulcers. Inwardly, though, it burned so fiercely that the patients could not bear to have even the lightest clothing or linen on them, and would rather be stark naked. What they wanted most was to throw themselves into cold water. Some of the neglected sick did so, plunging into the rain-tanks in their agony of unquenchable thirst; but it made no difference whether they drank little or much. On top of this, the wretched feeling of being unable to rest or sleep tormented them without ceasing. While the disease was at its height the body did not waste away, but withstood its ravages remarkably well. So when most patients died, on the seventh or eighth day, of the inward burning, they still had some strength left. But if they got past that stage and the disease descended further into the bowels, causing violent ulceration there with severe diarrhea, the resulting weakness was generally fatal. The disorder began in the head, ran its course from there through the whole body, and even where it did not kill, it left its mark on the extremities. It settled in the privy parts, the fingers and the toes, and many escaped with the loss of these, some also with the loss of their eyes. Others, on first recovering, were seized by a total loss of memory and knew neither themselves nor their friends.

note: Source hopes they were "safe from any disease whatsoever"; candidate narrows it to never dying of disease.
replacement: Such, then, setting aside the many peculiar variations from case to case, were the general features of the distemper. Meanwhile the city was free of all the usual disorders, or if any case occurred, it ended in this. Some died neglected, others in the midst of every attention. No remedy was found that could be used as a specific, for what helped in one case harmed in another. Strong and weak constitutions proved equally unable to resist; all alike were swept away, even those who were dieted with the utmost care. By far the most terrible feature of the malady was the dejection that came over anyone who felt himself sickening. The despair into which they instantly fell took away their power of resistance and made them a much easier prey to the disease. Besides this, there was the awful sight of men dying like sheep after catching the infection from nursing one another. This caused the greatest mortality. If they were afraid to visit one another, they perished from neglect; indeed many houses were emptied of their inmates for lack of a nurse. If, on the other hand, they ventured to visit, death was the result. This was especially so with those who made any claim to goodness. Honor made them spare themselves nothing in attending their friends in their houses, where even the members of the family were at last worn out by the moans of the dying and gave way to the force of the disaster. Yet it was those who had recovered from the disease who showed most compassion to the sick and the dying. They knew what it was from experience and now had no fear for themselves, for the same man was never attacked twice — never at least fatally. Such persons not only received the congratulations of others but, in the elation of the moment, half entertained the vain hope that they were safe from any disease whatsoever in the future.
